description_full: Silvercorp Metals Inc., together with its subsidiaries, acquires, explores, develops, and mines mineral properties in China. It explores for copper, silver, gold, lead, and zinc metals. The company was formerly known as SKN Resources Ltd. and changed its name to Silvercorp Metals Inc. in May 2005. Silvercorp Metals Inc. was founded in 2003 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

financial_summary: Silvercorp Metals Inc. is a small-cap basic materials business with a $2.0B market cap on $299M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 10% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 40%.

The business throws off $132M in free cash flow — roughly 44 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.76× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 3.9% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 35% operating margin runs 25pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.63x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 71% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 44% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 70% and a beta of 1.06, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.42 vs 5y 1.12), so read it loosely.
About $21.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 64% in the 2020 crash and 51% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 45% below its DCF fair value of $16.28, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 59%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $9.86 to $27.38 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 6.0 vs 8.5 and P/FCF 14.9 vs 22.8, richer on P/E 80.9 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 29% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $14.50 on average, 63% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 17% earns above the cost of capital of 10.0%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.27).
It runs a 40% gross margin and converts 44% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.76x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $241.9M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 11.1% over 3 years and 13.5% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 16.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.6% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 36.0% on average.
Analysts expect 94.1% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.9%, and institutions hold 75%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.3% (0.3% in dividends).
Short interest is elevated at 12.9% of the float, 15.3 days to cover.
people: With about 372 employees, each generates about $803K of revenue, 1.3x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 8.4% a year.
That works out to $356K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
